title: The Ice Pick Surgery That Won a Nobel Prize
style: Stylized realistic 3D CGI animation still, high-end animated explainer look, Pixar-meets-realism, cinematic soft lighting, detailed skin, hair and fabric, expressive faces, shallow depth of field, no text, no letters, no gore, vertical 9:16 framing.

sections.name: The Ice Pick Surgery That Won a Nobel Prize

lines.prompt: A 1940s psychiatric hospital hallway, a confident doctor in a suit and tie walking with a small leather bag

lines: In the 1940s, an American doctor named Walter Freeman travelled the country performing a ten minute brain operation.

lines.prompt: Close-up of a slim steel ice pick-like surgical tool on a metal tray, cold clinical lighting

lines: It was called the transorbital lobotomy. His tool looked a lot like an ice pick.

lines.prompt: A 1940s doctor seen from behind standing over a patient on a table, holding the tool near the patient's eye, nurses watching anxiously, no blood

lines: He pushed it in above the eye, and swept it side to side to cut connections in the front of the brain.

lines.prompt: A 1949 award ceremony, a Portuguese doctor in a tuxedo receiving a gold medal on a stage

lines: A different version of lobotomy even won its inventor a Nobel Prize, in 1949.

lines.prompt: A quiet hospital room with a patient sitting blankly by a window, a family member holding their hand

lines: Some patients became calmer. Many were left changed forever, and some died.

lines.prompt: A 1950s doctor holding a small bottle of pills, the ice pick tray pushed aside

lines: New medicines arrived in the 1950s, and lobotomy fell out of use. Freeman performed around three and a half thousand of them.
